pelvic-organ-prolapse.evidence: Not checked online; established urogynecology evaluation and conservative/surgical management.

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

perioperative-care.name: Perioperative care
perioperative-care.scope: Preoperative cardiac risk, pulmonary evaluation, surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, medication management, pain control
perioperative-care.core: Optimize active disease, estimate procedural and patient risk, and order testing only when the result could change perioperative management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **MI within 60 days**, decompensated HF → highest perioperative cardiac risk; older exam questions may expect MI within 6 months
Emergency, vascular or intrathoracic surgery; ischemic heart disease, heart failure, CKD, diabetes
Smoking, COPD, OSA, frailty, malnutrition and prior anesthesia complications

rows.label: Clues
items: Chest pain, new dyspnea, syncope or decompensated fluid overload require targeted evaluation
Poor functional capacity: inability to climb stairs or perform activities around 4 METs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Surgical stress raises myocardial oxygen demand; anesthesia can lower perfusion pressure
Sedation, pain and recumbency reduce ventilation and promote atelectasis and venous stasis
Surgical stress, pain, opioids → nonosmotic **ADH** release → transient oliguria with normal renal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RCRI/NSQIP** plus functional assessment; no routine stress test for low-risk surgery
Elevated risk, poor/unknown capacity → stress test if management changes; cannot exercise → **pharmacologic stress imaging**
ECG for cardiovascular symptoms; echo for new/worsening HF or suspected significant valve disease
No routine chest radiograph/spirometry without respiratory findings; assess airway and OSA history
Lung resection: **predicted postoperative FEV1** best predictor of complications; predicted postoperative FEV1 <30–40% → high risk, exercise testing before deciding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Active ACS, decompensated HF or unstable arrhythmia → defer elective surgery and stabilize
★ Continue chronic **beta blockers/statins**; do not start beta blockade on surgery day
Hold **SGLT2 inhibitors 3–4 days**; individualize GLP-1 drugs by aspiration risk; continue reduced basal insulin
★ **Cefazolin within 60 minutes** before incision; MRSA or severe beta-lactam allergy → vancomycin within 120 minutes
Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen, regional block, selective NSAID; add opioid by severity, respiratory monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial injury, AKI, delirium, pneumonia, VTE and surgical-site infection
Opioids aggravate OSA; excessive fluids can worsen pulmonary edema
New postoperative dyspnea, ↓basal breath sounds → chest radiograph first, before PE imaging or heparin

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lung expansion exercises, early mobilization, mechanical/pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis
Anticoagulation interruption individualized; bridging reserved for highest thrombotic risk
Chronic steroid exposure with adrenal suppression → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage
Usable gut → **enteral feeding**, including distal jejunostomy, over TPN

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anxiety-related dyspnea: normal cardiopulmonary evaluation
Stable chronic disease: baseline symptoms alone do not mandate cancellation

table.title: Postoperative pain
rows: Severe pain after major abdominal surgery

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings
Abrupt onset + AF, even with prior claudication → **embolus**, not in situ thrombosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle
Subclavian stenosis proximal to vertebral origin → arm exercise reverses ipsilateral vertebral flow; brachiocephalic lesion: right arm + carotid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; acute ischemia: bedside Doppler, **arteriography with runoff**
Subclavian steal → **compare BP in both arms** (gap >15 mm Hg); confirm with duplex or **MR angiography**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia with distal target → **surgical bypass** before amputation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin, vascular consultation** without awaiting imaging; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible or nonfunctional limb (nonambulatory, contractures) → primary amputation
Popliteal aneurysm: pulsatile popliteal mass, distal emboli; large → **tibial nerve compression** (posterior knee/calf pain)

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings
Thoracic outlet syndrome: symptoms on arm abduction, no posterior-circulation ischemia

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals
Calf claudication; normal femoral, weak pedal pulses
Arm-exercise dizziness/syncope or claudication; weak ipsilateral pulse

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

table.title: Difficult conversations
rows: Pause; allow feelings; schedule prompt follow-up
Voice openly in patient's presence; no covert action
Capable patient hides news from family
Encourage support; respect privacy; never lie to family
Child asks prognosis, parents forbid disclosure
Explore understanding; encourage talking with parents; never lie
Negotiate adherence contract; punitive control backfires
Fluent bilingual staff acceptable; never a child

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

physiologic-changes-of-aging.name: Physiologic changes of aging
physiologic-changes-of-aging.scope: Neurologic changes, sensory changes (presbyopia, presbycusis), sleep architecture changes (early wake, reduced total sleep), cardiovascular stiffening, renal decline, pulmonary compliance
physiologic-changes-of-aging.core: Normal aging reduces organ reserve; preserved everyday independence distinguishes expected slowing from disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: Gradual changes across systems; marked disability requires evaluation rather than attribution to age
Presbyopia: reduced accommodation; presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Slower processing and recall; **orientation and learned knowledge preserved**
★ Less slow-wave, more awakenings, earlier timing, less total sleep → **reassure**, no hypnotics
★ Isolated **↓ankle reflexes**, ↓toe vibration, impaired tandem, full strength → normal; no workup

rows.label: Use when
items: Reduced baroreflexes and maximal heart rate → orthostatic susceptibility, reduced exercise capacity
Lower renal clearance → adjust renally eliminated drugs despite normal-looking creatinine
Decreased vital capacity and cough reserve → greater respiratory illness vulnerability

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ **Arterial stiffness** → widened pulse pressure; ventricular relaxation slows
Reduced lung elastic recoil → increased lung compliance; chest wall compliance decreases
Declining concentration/dilution → fluid imbalance; reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Delirium, dementia, falls, incontinence** require evaluation; never inevitable normal aging
Depression or sedatives can explain daytime sleepiness; severe insomnia needs investigation
Unilateral hearing loss, focal weakness, **rotatory nystagmus**, rapid memory loss → disease workup

physiologic-changes-of-aging.evidence: Not checked online; established geriatric physiology.

pityriasis-rosea.name: Pityriasis rosea
pityriasis-rosea.scope: Herald patch, Christmas tree distribution, collarette of scale, viral prodrome, distinction from secondary syphilis, symptomatic management
pityriasis-rosea.core: Single herald patch followed days later by smaller oval scaly plaques in a Christmas tree pattern.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Most common in adolescents and young adults

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Collarette of scale** just inside plaque edge; lesions follow cleavage lines on trunk
Possible viral prodrome; pruritus variable; palms, soles and mucosa usually spared

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Self-limited papulosquamous eruption; suspected viral reactivation, unproven cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis with typical evolution and distribution
Atypical rash, palmoplantar lesions, or sexual risk → syphilis serology
KOH scraping if annular plaque could represent dermatophyte infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reassurance: spontaneous resolution usually within 6–8 weeks
★ Pruritus → topical hydrocortisone or oral cetirizine; emollients
Severe widespread eruption → consider acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Temporary postinflammatory pigment changes, especially in darker skin

rows.label: Mimics
items: Secondary syphilis: palmoplantar lesions, generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous patches
Tinea corporis: advancing outer scale, central clearing, positive KOH
Guttate psoriasis: drop-like lesions after streptococcal pharyngitis, no preceding solitary plaque

pityriasis-rosea.evidence: Checked American Academy of Dermatology pityriasis rosea diagnosis and treatment guidance.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.scope: Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration, atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma)
pneumonia.core: Acute lower respiratory infection with a new infiltrate; severity, acquisition setting, and resistance risks determine disposition and empiric antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, COPD, age, immunosuppression
Dysphagia, absent gag/cough (stroke, dementia, Parkinson), impaired consciousness → aspiration
HAP ≥48 hours hospitalized; VAP ≥48 hours after intubation
Prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics → resistant pathogens

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, cough, sputum, focal crackles; older adults: confusion; children: lower-lobe disease may refer abdominal pain
★ Severe: **hypoxemia, hypotension, tachypnea**, multilobar disease; ventilation or pressors → ICU
Legionella: water exposure, diarrhea, hyponatremia; Mycoplasma: school-age/young adult, indolent dry cough, cold agglutinins
Immunocompromised, diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar infiltrates, exertional hypoxemia → **Pneumocystis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar inflammation/exudate → shunt and impaired oxygenation
Chemical aspiration pneumonitis: sterile gastric injury; severity tracks **volume and acidity**; rapid improvement possible

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CXR** first; CT if strong suspicion despite nondiagnostic radiograph
**CURB-65** 0–1 or low PSI → outpatient; severe CAP → blood/sputum cultures, Legionella antigen ± PCR
Low procalcitonin alone does not justify withholding initial antibiotics in radiographically confirmed bacterial CAP
Gram-positive lancet diplococci → **S pneumoniae**: commonest CAP; lobar consolidation, high fever, often post-viral URI
Small gram-negative coccobacilli, smoker/COPD → **H influenzae**

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen, fluids for hypoperfusion; drain empyema; narrow antibiotics to cultures
★ Aspiration pneumonia: usual CAP coverage; **add anaerobic coverage only for abscess/empyema**
Anaerobes: **ampicillin-sulbactam**; older exam questions may expect **clindamycin**, even without abscess
Stable nonsevere CAP: ATS 2025 permits 3–4 days; classic ≥5-day rule remains for severe disease
★ Severe noninfluenza CAP → consider **systemic corticosteroids**; nonsevere CAP → avoid routine steroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema, bacteremia, respiratory failure, sepsis
S aureus: postinfluenza necrotizing pneumonia; child failing amoxicillin, dense consolidation/effusion
Aspiration (alcoholism, intubation) → **lung abscess**: dependent-segment cavity, air-fluid level, foul sputum
Antibiotic exposure → C difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, smoking cessation, swallowing evaluation
Aspiration/VAP prevention: head elevation 30–45°, oral care, early liberation from ventilation

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: thrombotic risk, pleuritic pain, no infectious source
HF: bilateral edema, elevated JVP, cardiac dysfunction

table.title: Empiric adult regimens
rows: Amoxicillin/clavulanate + azithromycin; doxycycline alternative; or levofloxacin
Antipseudomonal: cefepime, ceftazidime, or piperacillin/tazobactam; usually 7 days

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.name: Population health and quality improvement
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.scope: Program evaluation, outcome and process measures, health equity, PDSA cycles
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.core: Improve care for a defined population through measurable aims, iterative system changes, and attention to unequal access and outcomes.

rows.label: Principle
items: Population denominator includes eligible people missing visits, not only those receiving care
Equity: stratify outcomes by language, race/ethnicity, geography, disability, insurance, deprivation
Greater relative **primary care investment** improves population health, reduces disparities

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Define **measurable aim**, population, baseline, timeframe; engage patients/frontline staff
★ **PDSA**: plan small change → do → study results → act/adapt before scaling
Stratify measures, address interpreter/transport/cost barriers, monitor unintended consequences

rows.label: Don't
items: Do not assume a favorable outcome proves causation without comparison and context
Avoid blaming individuals for failures created by unreliable workflows

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Run/control charts distinguish routine common-cause variation from special-cause signals over time
Program evaluation: reach, fidelity, effectiveness, cost, sustainability versus original goals
Education program → measure knowledge/behavior change; small cohort cannot detect morbidity/mortality

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Process success ≠ patient benefit**; assess both and choose valid denominators
★ **Risk adjustment** improves comparison; also report disparities so adjustment cannot conceal inequity
Before–after improvement may reflect secular trends, case-mix change, regression to mean

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.evidence: Established quality-improvement and program-evaluation principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

postpartum-care.name: Postpartum care
postpartum-care.scope: Normal puerperal changes, lochia, uterine involution, perineal and cesarean wound healing, breastfeeding, postpartum depression screening, routine postpartum visit
postpartum-care.core: Postpartum care is an ongoing assessment of recovery, mood, infant feeding, contraception, and chronic disease after every birth.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ All postpartum patients; assess support, sleep, safety, sexual health, and reproductive goals

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Contact within **3 weeks**; comprehensive visit by **12 weeks**, with earlier risk-based review
Hypertensive disorder → BP within 7–10 days; severe hypertension → within 72 hours

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Edinburgh or PHQ-9 depression screen; assess suicidality directly after positive self-harm response
BP, bleeding, fundal tenderness; inspect perineum/incision for erythema, drainage, separation
Observe latch/milk transfer; frequent feeds, lactation support; cracked nipples → correct positioning

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Heavy bleeding (pad soaked <1 hour), fever, dyspnea, severe headache → urgent evaluation
Mood screen positive → diagnostic interview, psychotherapy/SSRI; psychosis → emergency hospitalization
Increasing wound pain/purulence → evaluate infection; breast fluctuance → ultrasound for abscess

rows.label: Traps
items: Ovulation may precede first period; discuss contraception before discharge
Lactational contraception: amenorrhea, exclusive frequent breastfeeding, infant <6 months
Postpartum hypertension and cardiomyopathy can first appear after discharge

table.title: Expected recovery
rows: Red rubra → pink serosa → white/yellow alba
Descends daily; near prepregnancy size by 6 weeks
Pain improves; pulling normal if intact; keep clean
Early cramping and fluid loss; breastfeeding intensifies cramping

postpartum-care.evidence: Visit timing checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG postpartum care](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2018/05/optimizing-postpartum-care); normal physiology established teaching.

primary-headaches.name: Primary headaches
primary-headaches.scope: Migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication-overuse headache, red flags
primary-headaches.core: Recurrent stereotyped headaches with normal neurologic examination favor a primary syndrome; a new dangerous pattern requires secondary-cause evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, sleep disruption, stress, hormonal fluctuation; alcohol triggers cluster bouts
Frequent rescue analgesic use promotes chronic daily headache

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Thunderclap, fever, papilledema, focal deficit, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum** → evaluate secondary cause
New headache after age 50, positional/Valsalva provocation, progressive change also concerning
Medication overuse: headache ≥15 days/month with sustained frequent acute-drug exposure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Migraine: trigeminovascular/CGRP signaling; aura: cortical spreading depolarization, visual → contralateral occipital lobe
Cluster: hypothalamic/autonomic activation; overuse sustains sensitization and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical stable primary pattern + normal exam → **no routine neuroimaging**
Thunderclap → head CT; negative with persistent SAH concern → LP or CTA
MRI for concerning nonemergent progressive patterns; fundoscopy and full neurologic examination
Overuse >3 months: triptans/opioids/combinations ≥10 days/month; acetaminophen/NSAIDs ≥15 days/month

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe migraine → **sumatriptan + naproxen**, metoclopramide for nausea; avoid triptans with ischemic vascular disease
Frequent migraine → propranolol, topiramate, CGRP drugs; pregnancy → **acetaminophen**; no ergots, topiramate, valproate
★ Cluster attack → **100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan**; prevention with verapamil, ECG monitoring
Tension headache → acetaminophen/NSAID; recurrent chronic disease → amitriptyline, behavioral treatment
Medication overuse → withdraw culprit, start prevention; taper opioids/barbiturates rather than abrupt withdrawal

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic migraine, functional disability, status migrainosus; analgesic toxicity
Estrogen-containing contraception increases stroke concern in migraine with aura
Triptan + **ergotamine within 24 hours** → additive vasoconstriction: prolonged vasospasm, MI, stroke

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Regular sleep/meals, exercise, headache diary**, limit rescue-drug days
Avoid opioids for routine primary headache; identify personal rather than universal dietary triggers
Migraine escalation after starting estrogen, normal exam → **stop estrogen** before imaging or added analgesics

rows.label: Mimics
items: GCA: age >50, jaw claudication/visual symptoms
Acute glaucoma: red painful eye, halos, high pressure; sinusitis: purulence and objective sinus findings

primary-headaches.evidence: Not checked online; established headache classification and generalist management.

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists
DiGeorge: 3rd/4th **pharyngeal pouch** failure → absent thymus, hypocalcemia, conotruncal defects, T-cell infections
ADA deficiency: autosomal recessive SCID; toxic deoxyadenosine destroys T and B cells

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vertical HIV: bacterial infections + zoster, nodes, maternal opportunistic infection; low CD4, positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

primary-immunodeficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical immunology teaching.

prostatitis.name: Prostatitis
prostatitis.scope: Acute bacterial prostatitis, chronic bacterial prostatitis, chronic pelvic pain syndrome, tender prostate, fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX, prostatic abscess
prostatitis.core: Pelvic or perineal pain with urinary symptoms; distinguish acute infection, recurrent bacterial disease, and chronic noninfectious pelvic pain.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Urinary tract instrumentation, catheterization, bladder outlet obstruction, recurrent UTI; E. coli most typical
Recent prostate biopsy increases resistant gram-negative risk; sexual exposure may indicate gonorrhea/chlamydia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Acute disease: fever, chills, dysuria, retention, and **tender boggy prostate** on gentle examination
Chronic bacterial disease: recurrent UTIs with the same organism, intermittent symptoms between episodes
Persistent fever despite antibiotics or focal fluctuance suggests abscess; hypotension → sepsis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ascending bacteria or infected urine reflux into prostatic ducts → inflammation and tissue infection
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome: multifactorial pelvic floor/neuromuscular pain without demonstrable ongoing bacterial infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis and urine culture** before antibiotics; blood cultures if febrile/systemically ill
Avoid vigorous prostatic massage during acute infection → bacteremia risk; PSA transiently rises, not diagnostic
Sexually active, pyuria + negative routine culture → **Chlamydia**; urine NAAT
Persistent fever >36–48 hours → CT or transrectal ultrasound
Chronic uncertainty → pre/post-massage urine cultures after acute infection excluded

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe acute illness → IV **ceftriaxone** or broader culture-informed coverage; fluids and hospitalization
Stable acute infection → ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX if susceptible, **2–4 weeks**; nitrofurantoin penetrates prostate poorly
Chronic bacterial infection → culture-directed fluoroquinolone, usually **4–6 weeks**
★ CPPS → **pelvic floor physical therapy**, NSAIDs, tamsulosin for voiding symptoms; avoid repeated empiric antibiotics
Retention → urology-guided drainage, often suprapubic; abscess → drainage plus antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Urosepsis, urinary retention, prostatic abscess, recurrent bacterial infection
Fluoroquinolones → tendinopathy, neuropathy, QT prolongation; TMP-SMX → hyperkalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Address obstruction and urinary tract abnormalities; minimize avoidable instrumentation and catheter duration
Sexual risk counseling and partner treatment when an STI is identified

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cystitis: no systemic toxicity or prostatic tenderness
BPH: chronic obstructive symptoms with smooth enlarged, nontender prostate
Prostate cancer: hard nodularity; reassess persistent PSA elevation after inflammation resolves

pubertal-development.name: Pubertal development
pubertal-development.scope: Tanner stages, normal thelarche vs breast mass, premature adrenarche, precocious puberty, constitutional delay of growth and puberty
pubertal-development.core: Interpret sexual maturation by sequence, age, growth velocity, and bone age; isolated benign variants lack progressive gonadal activation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constitutional delay often familial; chronic illness, undernutrition, excess exercise delay maturation
CNS lesions, gonadal/adrenal hormone excess, exogenous sex steroids can cause early puberty

rows.label: Clues
items: Girls: breast budding precedes peak growth, then menarche about 2–3 years later
Boys: testes enlarge before penile growth; pubic hair reflects adrenarche, not necessarily gonadarche
★ Asymmetric tender **subareolar breast bud** at expected age usually normal; hard eccentric mass needs evaluation
Rapid height acceleration, advancing secondary characteristics, neurologic symptoms → pathologic early maturation concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central puberty: hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility → LH/FSH → gonadal steroids
Adrenarche produces adrenal androgens independently; peripheral hormone excess suppresses pituitary gonadotropins
Immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis → irregular anovulatory cycles, normal for 2–3 years after menarche
Virilized boy with **prepubertal testes** → peripheral androgen, usually adrenal; central puberty enlarges testes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Precocious: secondary sexual development **before 8 years girls or 9 years boys**
★ Delayed: **no breasts by 13**, no testes ≥4 mL by 14; evaluate absent menarche by 15
Growth chart, Tanner examination, bone age; LH/FSH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH selected by pattern
Central precocity → pubertal basal/stimulated LH; brain MRI especially boys, young girls, neurologic signs
Peripheral pattern → targeted adrenal/gonadal tests/imaging; isolated adrenarche requires exclusion of rapid virilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Progressive central precocity → **GnRH agonist**; treat CNS cause when present
Peripheral precocity → remove hormone source or treat tumor/adrenal disorder; GnRH agonist alone ineffective
Constitutional delay → reassurance, follow growth; distress → specialist-guided brief sex-steroid course
Benign premature thelarche/adrenarche → observe progression; no automatic hormonal treatment
Pubertal gynecomastia, unilateral or bilateral, smooth subareolar → **reassurance**; no labs/biopsy; carcinoma very rare

rows.label: Complications
items: Early epiphyseal closure → reduced adult height; psychosocial distress
Missed hypogonadism → impaired bone accrual; untreated CNS/tumor cause may progress

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, manage chronic disease, avoid household hormone exposure; serial growth surveillance
Normal puberty + moodiness, mild parent conflict → **puberty education** for child, parents; no drug testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary gonadal failure: high LH/FSH, low sex steroids
Permanent central hypogonadism: absent progression rather than eventual familial catch-up
Familial short stature: short parents, bone age matches chronologic age; constitutional delay: **delayed bone age**

table.title: Tanner staging anchors
rows: Further enlargement; menarche usually within 1–2 years

pubertal-development.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric endocrine timing and Tanner staging.

pulmonary-hypertension.name: Pulmonary hypertension
pulmonary-hypertension.scope: WHO groups 1-5 (PAH, left heart disease, lung disease/hypoxia, CTEPH, multifactorial), cor pulmonale, echocardiography, right heart catheterization, endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors
pulmonary-hypertension.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart failure with elevated pulmonary pressures requires hemodynamic classification before vasodilator treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Connective-tissue disease, congenital shunts, portal hypertension, HIV, methamphetamine → PAH
Left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia or prior pulmonary embolism are common secondary contexts

rows.label: Clues
items: Loud P2, RV heave, tricuspid regurgitation murmur; exertional chest pain or presyncope
JVD, hepatomegaly and edema → right-heart failure/cor pulmonale
Severe dyspnea with relatively preserved spirometry or low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary vascular resistance or elevated left filling pressure increases RV afterload
Sustained pressure overload → RV hypertrophy, dilation, reduced output and systemic venous congestion
Chronic alveolar hypoxia (COPD, OSA) → **pulmonary vasoconstriction** and remodeling → raised vascular resistance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography** estimates probability and evaluates RV/left-heart function; not definitive pressure diagnosis
★ **Right-heart catheterization: mean PAP >20 mm Hg** at rest confirms PH
Precapillary: wedge ≤15 mm Hg and **PVR >2 Wood units**; postcapillary: wedge >15
★ **V/Q scan** screens CTEPH; normal perfusion essentially excludes chronic thromboembolic disease
PFT/DLCO, chest CT, sleep evaluation, HIV/autoimmune testing by history; vasoreactivity testing in selected PAH

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen for hypoxemia, diuresis for congestion; treat underlying disease and refer confirmed PAH/CTEPH
★ PAH → specialist **endothelin antagonist + PDE-5 inhibitor**; high-risk disease → parenteral prostacyclin
Vasoreactive idiopathic/heritable/drug-associated PAH → selected high-dose calcium-channel blocker; not empiric treatment
CTEPH → lifelong anticoagulation and pulmonary endarterectomy if operable; selected balloon angioplasty or riociguat
Do not routinely use PAH vasodilators for left-heart/lung-disease PH; PDE-5 drugs cannot combine with nitrates/riociguat

rows.label: Complications
items: RV failure, arrhythmia, syncope and death; pregnancy carries substantial maternal risk in PAH
Endothelin antagonists are teratogenic; some require liver monitoring

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid methamphetamine, address thromboembolic risk; vaccination, supervised exercise, pregnancy/contraception counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: HFpEF: elevated wedge pressure identifies postcapillary cause
Deconditioning/anemia: no catheter-confirmed pulmonary pressure elevation

renin-angiotensin-system-inhibitors.name: Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors
renin-angiotensin-system-inhibitors.scope: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, direct renin inhibitors, hyperkalemia, angioedema, cough
renin-angiotensin-system-inhibitors.core: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aliskiren interrupt the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis at different steps.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ **ACE inhibitor or ARB**: hypertension with albuminuric CKD; post-MI ventricular dysfunction
HFrEF: ACE inhibitor/ARB when sacubitril-valsartan cannot be used; aliskiren lacks outcome benefits

rows.label: Mechanism
items: ACE cleaves **C-terminal dipeptide** of angiotensin I → angiotensin II; inhibitors block this step
Efferent arteriolar dilation → ↓glomerular filtration pressure; ↓aldosterone → potassium retention

rows.label: Adverse
items: Hypotension, AKI during hypovolemia; modest stable creatinine rise expected
★ **Angioedema → stop ACE inhibitor permanently**, assess/protect airway; possible even after years

rows.label: Avoid
items: ★ **Pregnancy**, bilateral renal artery stenosis, uncontrolled hyperkalemia
Prior ACE angioedema → no ACE inhibitor; subsequent ARB needs individualized assessment

rows.label: Interactions
items: ★ **Never combine ACE inhibitor, ARB, or aliskiren**; additive kidney injury and hyperkalemia
Potassium supplements, spironolactone, trimethoprim → ↑K; NSAID + diuretic → AKI
Sacubitril-valsartan requires **36-hour ACE inhibitor washout**; RAAS blockade can raise lithium

rows.label: Monitor
items: Baseline BP, creatinine, K → repeat within **2–4 weeks** after initiation/dose increase
Creatinine rise >30% → investigate volume depletion, NSAIDs, renovascular disease; reassess drug

rows.label: Traps
items: Advanced CKD alone → no automatic discontinuation; manage reversible hyperkalemia contributors first

restless-legs-syndrome.name: Restless legs syndrome
restless-legs-syndrome.scope: URGE criteria, iron deficiency association (ferritin <75), secondary causes (pregnancy, uremia, neuropathy), nonpharmacologic measures, iron replacement, dopamine agonists, alpha-2-delta ligands
restless-legs-syndrome.core: An uncomfortable urge to move the legs during rest, relieved by movement and worse in the evening, disrupts sleep.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Iron deficiency, pregnancy, CKD/uremia, family history; neuropathy may coexist
Antihistamines, serotonergic antidepressants, dopamine antagonists, caffeine, alcohol and untreated OSA exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually bilateral deep crawling/aching sensations; neurologic examination often normal in primary disease
Repetitive sleep-related leg movements may coexist but are not required for diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Low brain iron and altered dopamine signaling; normal ferritin can mask functional iron deficiency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical URGE criteria**; symptoms not solely explained by cramps, posture or another disorder
★ Check **ferritin + transferrin saturation**, CBC and renal function; PSG usually unnecessary
Evaluate pregnancy, neuropathy and medications; isolated periodic limb movements alone ≠ RLS

rows.label: Tx
items: Regular sleep, moderate exercise, stretching/massage; remove exacerbating agents and treat OSA
★ **Iron replacement** if ferritin ≤75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation <20%
Oral ferrous sulfate when suitable; ferritin 75–100 or poor absorption/response → IV iron, often ferric carboxymaltose
★ Persistent symptoms → **gabapentin, pregabalin or gabapentin enacarbil**; adjust for renal function

rows.label: Complications
items: Insomnia, daytime fatigue, mood impairment; gabapentinoids cause sedation, edema and falls
Dopaminergic augmentation: earlier, stronger symptoms, spread to arms; impulse-control problems possible

rows.label: Prevention
items: Investigate and correct iron-loss source; repeat iron indices during replacement
Pregnancy: prioritize nonpharmacologic measures and iron; individualized obstetric medication review

rows.label: Mimics
items: Akathisia: generalized inner restlessness, medication-related, little circadian pattern
Nocturnal cramps: focal painful contraction, palpable muscle tightening
Neuropathy: persistent sensory symptoms not reliably relieved by movement

table.title: Dopaminergic drugs: AASM 2025
rows: Discouraged routinely; selected short-term use possible
Specialist gradual taper; avoid escalation or abrupt withdrawal

rh-alloimmunization.name: Rh alloimmunization
rh-alloimmunization.scope: Rh(D) and other red cell alloimmunization (Kell, Duffy), anti-D immune globulin prophylaxis, indirect Coombs titer monitoring, fetomaternal hemorrhage (Kleihauer-Betke), middle cerebral artery Doppler for fetal anemia
rh-alloimmunization.core: Maternal IgG against fetal red-cell antigens crosses the placenta, causing fetal anemia, hydrops, and neonatal hemolysis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Antigen-negative mother/positive fetus; prior pregnancy, transfusion, bleeding, trauma, invasive procedures
Anti-D, anti-Kell, and anti-Duffy clinically significant; ABO incompatibility usually milder

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic mother; fetal ascites, skin edema, placentomegaly, cardiomegaly
Neonate: early jaundice, pallor, reticulocytosis, **positive direct Coombs**; severe disease → cardiovascular collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: First exposure sensitizes; subsequent antigen exposure produces an anamnestic response
Kell antibodies additionally suppress erythropoiesis; low titers can still cause severe disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First prenatal visit: ABO/Rh type + **indirect Coombs**; repeat before routine antenatal prophylaxis
Antibody → **paternal antigen typing**; negative (certain paternity) → no fetal risk; else fetal typing, titers
★ Critical titer, often **1:16**, or previously affected pregnancy → middle cerebral artery Doppler
MCA peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM → fetal blood sampling; Kell warrants specialist surveillance
Kleihauer-Betke quantifies hemorrhage for dosing: **300 µg covers 30 mL fetal whole blood**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe preterm fetal anemia → **intrauterine transfusion**; near term → delivery
Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → phototherapy; severe hemolysis → exchange transfusion

rows.label: Complications
items: High-output heart failure, stillbirth, bilirubin encephalopathy, delayed neonatal anemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Unsensitized Rh-negative mother: **anti-D immune globulin** at 28 weeks and within 72 hours postpartum
Sensitizing event → dose now; lasts ~12 weeks, repeat at 28; postpartum only if Rh-positive/unknown infant
★ Established anti-D sensitization → prophylaxis ineffective; no equivalent prophylaxis for Kell/Duffy
ACOG 2024: routine Rh testing/prophylaxis may be forgone for abortion/loss before 12 weeks

rows.label: Mimics
items: Parvovirus: nonimmune hydrops with negative maternal antibody screen
ABO hemolysis: may affect first pregnancy; fetal hydrops uncommon

rh-alloimmunization.evidence: Prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG Rh guidance](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/the-rh-factor-how-it-can-affect-your-pregnancy), [2024 update](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000005733); remaining content established teaching.

rhabdomyolysis.name: Rhabdomyolysis
rhabdomyolysis.scope: Trauma, crush injury, prolonged immobilization, statins, seizures, elevated CK, myoglobinuria (blood on dipstick without RBCs), acute tubular necrosis, aggressive IV saline hydration
rhabdomyolysis.core: Acute skeletal muscle breakdown releases myoglobin and electrolytes; recognize pigment nephropathy early and restore renal perfusion before kidney failure develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Crush injury, prolonged immobilization**, compartment syndrome, ischemia/reperfusion
Seizures, strenuous exercise, heatstroke, cocaine; statins, especially with interacting drugs
Hypokalemia, infections, alcohol intoxication; pressure injury during unconsciousness

rows.label: Clues
items: Muscle pain, weakness, swelling; dark urine possible, but classic triad often incomplete
↑K, ↑phosphate, early ↓Ca; AST may rise from muscle rather than liver
Tense painful compartment, pain with passive stretch, sensory change → concurrent limb emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Myocyte necrosis → pigment-mediated tubular injury and casts, amplified by hypovolemia and aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK >5 times upper limit**, often >1,000 U/L; trend until clearly declining
★ Urine dipstick **heme positive with few/no RBCs** → myoglobin; negative result cannot exclude
Electrolytes, creatinine, ECG, urine output; CK magnitude supports risk assessment, not dialysis alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early **IV normal saline**; titrate to urine output 1–3 mL/kg/hour, avoiding overload
Stop culprit; treat heatstroke/seizures; compartment syndrome → emergency fasciotomy
Hyperkalemic ECG changes → IV calcium, insulin/dextrose; dialysis for refractory electrolyte/volume/acid-base disturbances
★ **No routine bicarbonate or mannitol** for AKI prevention; anuria → reassess fluids, renal consultation
Asymptomatic hypocalcemia → avoid replacement; symptomatic tetany or arrhythmia → calcium

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute tubular necrosis, dangerous arrhythmias, disseminated intravascular coagulation
Recovery phase → rebound hypercalcemia; excessive fluids with renal failure → pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration and gradual exercise progression; avoid exertion during severe heat or illness
Review statin interactions, especially macrolides/gemfibrozil; pressure relief during prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hematuria: numerous RBCs on microscopy
Hemolysis: heme-positive urine with anemia, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin rather than marked CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: subacute proximal weakness without acute toxic/traumatic trigger

rhabdomyolysis.evidence: Fluid targets and bicarbonate guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAST consensus, 2022](https://tsaco.bmj.com/content/7/1/e000836.full.pdf).

rheumatoid-arthritis.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
rheumatoid-arthritis.scope: Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, anti-CCP and RF, DMARDs (methotrexate, biologics), extra-articular manifestations, Felty syndrome, cervical spine subluxation
rheumatoid-arthritis.core: Persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness and improvement with activity; early disease-modifying treatment prevents erosions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Female sex, smoking, family history, HLA-DRB1 susceptibility; onset often middle adulthood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Boggy swelling of **MCP, PIP, wrists**; DIP joints usually spared
Ulnar deviation, swan-neck/boutonnière deformities; subcutaneous nodules and constitutional symptoms
Extra-articular: pleuritis, interstitial lung disease, episcleritis/scleritis, pericarditis, neuropathy
★ **Felty syndrome**: established erosive disease + splenomegaly + neutropenia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoimmune synovial inflammation → pannus, cartilage destruction, marginal bone erosion
TNF and other inflammatory cytokines drive articular and systemic injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical synovitis → **anti-CCP, RF, ESR/CRP**; anti-CCP more specific, negative serology not exclusionary
Hand/foot radiographs: periarticular osteopenia, uniform narrowing, erosions; early films can be normal
Acute single hot joint → arthrocentesis to exclude infection or crystals before attributing symptoms
Neck pain, neurologic symptoms, or suspected instability before anesthesia → cervical imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Methotrexate + folate** first-line for moderate/high activity; hydroxychloroquine reasonable for low activity
Treat to remission/low activity; inadequate response → add biologic, often TNF inhibitor
NSAIDs relieve symptoms without preventing joint damage; glucocorticoid bridge only briefly when necessary
Methotrexate: avoid pregnancy, significant liver disease; monitor CBC, creatinine, LFTs
TNF inhibitors: avoid active infection, advanced heart failure, demyelinating disease

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Atlantoaxial subluxation** → cord compression; protect cervical spine during airway management
Accelerated cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, secondary amyloidosis; immunosuppression → serious infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, occupational/physical rehabilitation; assess bone and cardiovascular risk
Screen TB and hepatitis B before biologics; update vaccines before immunosuppression

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteoarthritis: bony DIP/first CMC enlargement, brief stiffness
Psoriatic arthritis: dactylitis, nail pitting, asymmetric or DIP involvement
SLE arthritis: usually nonerosive, rash/cytopenias, disease-specific autoantibodies

routine-prenatal-care.name: Routine prenatal care and early pregnancy
routine-prenatal-care.scope: Pregnancy diagnosis (beta-hCG), initial prenatal assessment, routine first-trimester screening, aneuploidy screening
routine-prenatal-care.core: Confirm and date pregnancy, assess maternal risks, offer one aneuploidy-screening strategy or diagnostic testing, and arrange time-sensitive prenatal studies.

rows.label: Who
items: All pregnancies; review obstetric history, drugs, illness, substance use, violence, family history
Offer carrier screening and genetic counseling; discuss patient preferences and right to decline

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Early visit: urine hCG confirms pregnancy; serum quantitative hCG for uncertain/complicated cases
★ First-trimester **ultrasound crown–rump length** best establishes gestational age
Serum screen 10–13 6/7 weeks; NT 11–13 6/7; cfDNA from 10 weeks

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Initial **CBC, ABO/Rh, antibody screen, urine culture**; HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, HCV, rubella immunity
GC/chlamydia by age/risk; offer one aneuploidy strategy regardless of maternal age
Anatomy ultrasound 18–22 weeks; AFP for open neural tube defects when not otherwise assessed

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Abnormal screen → counseling, ultrasound, **CVS/amniocentesis** before irreversible decisions
CVS: 10–13 weeks; amniocentesis: ≥15 weeks; neither automatically required after negative screening
Rh-negative, unsensitized → anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks and after sensitizing events

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **cfDNA is screening**, not diagnostic; does not screen open neural tube defects
Single hCG value cannot establish viability or location; pain/bleeding → ectopic evaluation
Folate before conception/early gestation; avoid alcohol, tobacco, teratogens; no live vaccines

table.title: Early and routine pregnancy calls
rows: Nausea, irregular bleeding or amenorrhea, even premenarche
Missed menses, urinary frequency, friable cervix, enlarged uterus
Brief sharp movement-triggered lower-quadrant pain, normal vitals
No added preterm, fluid, or placental risk

schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.name: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.scope: Brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, mesolimbic dopamine
schizophrenia-spectrum-disorders.core: Psychosis with impaired reality testing: distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders by duration, functional decline, and the relationship between mood episodes and psychosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, neurodevelopmental vulnerability; adolescent cannabis exposure increases risk
Typical onset late adolescence/early adulthood; exclude stimulant, hallucinogen, medication, and neurologic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior; negative symptoms: avolition, alogia, flat affect
★ At least **two core symptoms**, including delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, for active-phase diagnosis
Suicidality, dangerous commands or inability to eat → urgent safety assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **↑Mesolimbic dopamine** → positive symptoms; mesocortical → negative symptoms, early working-memory deficits
D2 blockade reduces psychosis but nigrostriatal/tuberoinfundibular effects cause EPS and hyperprolactinemia
Structural correlate: **enlarged lateral and third ventricles**, reduced cortical volume

rows.label: Dx
items: Clinical history, collateral information, mental status; assess mood timeline and substance exposure
First episode → CBC/CMP, TSH, toxicology; HIV/syphilis or neuroimaging for relevant risks/atypical neurologic findings
★ **Schizoaffective**: ≥2 weeks psychosis without mood episode; mood episodes occupy most illness duration

rows.label: Tx
items: Safety crisis → hospitalization; acute agitation → de-escalation, then medication if needed
★ **Risperidone, aripiprazole or olanzapine** + coordinated specialty care, family education, CBT, supported employment
Schizoaffective depressive/bipolar subtype → add antidepressant or mood stabilizer according to mood syndrome
★ Failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials or persistent substantial suicide risk → **clozapine**
Adherence difficulty → long-acting injectable (haloperidol decanoate); catatonia → lorazepam, then ECT if refractory

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, homelessness, substance use, cardiometabolic disease; antipsychotics → metabolic syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, NMS
Clozapine → neutropenia, myocarditis, severe constipation; monitor ANC and symptoms

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid cannabis/stimulants; maintenance medication, relapse planning reduce recurrence
Monitor weight, BP, glucose, lipids; address tobacco use and cardiovascular risk
**High expressed emotion** (family criticism, hostility) → relapse; family therapy reduces recurrence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mood disorder with psychosis: psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes
Delirium: fluctuating attention/awareness and acute medical cause
Delusional disorder: ≥1 month delusions with otherwise relatively preserved function, limited other psychotic symptoms
Substance/medication-induced psychosis: recent stimulants (mydriasis, tremor) or corticosteroids, intact orientation

secondary-hypertension.name: Secondary hypertension
secondary-hypertension.scope: Renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta, diagnostic workup
secondary-hypertension.core: Abrupt, unusually young, severe, or resistant hypertension suggests a treatable secondary driver.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Renal stenosis: older smoker → atherosclerotic **lipid plaque**; young/middle-aged woman → **fibromuscular dysplasia** (medial hyperplasia, renal + carotid)
Renal disease, adrenal tumors, sleep apnea
NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, stimulants, glucocorticoids, licorice; medication nonadherence can mimic resistance

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis** → aldosterone excess, primary or renovascular; normal K does not exclude it
**Abdominal bruit**, diffuse atherosclerosis, late abrupt worsening, small unilateral kidney → renal artery stenosis
Flash pulmonary edema or creatinine rise >30% after ACE inhibitor/ARB → renovascular disease
**Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations** → pheochromocytoma; cushingoid appearance, upper-body hypertension guide testing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Renal hypoperfusion → juxtaglomerular **renin** → RAAS; ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction → ↓renal flow, ↓GFR across stenosis
Autonomous aldosterone → distal sodium absorption, potassium loss, low renin; pressure natriuresis escape prevents edema
Adrenal medullary catecholamine or cortisol excess, aortic obstruction, or nocturnal hypoxia increases vascular pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **home/ambulatory BP**, adherence, cuff technique; BMP, urinalysis, creatinine, TSH
Sleep-apnea symptoms → polysomnography; abnormal urinary sediment → renal ultrasound and kidney evaluation
★ Biochemical testing precedes adrenal imaging; correct hypokalemia and account for interfering medications
Endocrine Society 2025: suggest **aldosterone screening for all hypertension**, conditional on resources

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Primary aldosteronism: unilateral → **adrenalectomy**; bilateral → spironolactone/eplerenone
Renovascular atherosclerosis → medical risk reduction; revascularize selected recurrent pulmonary edema or refractory disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia → angioplasty; critical bilateral renal stenosis → avoid ACE inhibitor/ARB
★ Pheochromocytoma: **alpha blockade before beta blockade**, volume expansion, then surgery
Treat cortisol source, repair significant coarctation, use CPAP for OSA; stop contributing drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, heart failure, CKD, retinopathy
Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can cause catecholamine crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor renal function/K after RAAS blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists
Genetic evaluation/family screening for suspected hereditary pheochromocytoma or congenital aortic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: normal out-of-office readings
Essential hypertension: gradual course without specific endocrine/renal clues

table.title: Targeted workup
rows: Selective suppression test; CT/adrenal venous sampling
Plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines

secondary-hypertension.evidence: Aldosterone screening checked 2026-10-30: [Endocrine Society 2025](https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/primary-aldosteronism-2); other causes: established teaching.

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk
Procedure bleeding: thoracentesis → intercostal artery, hemothorax; splenectomy → hemoperitoneum, left shoulder pain

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: **lost sympathetic tone** → hypotension, bradycardia or no tachycardia, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid
Warm sepsis: high output, **high mixed venous O2**; pump failure: low contractility, congestion; hypovolemia: low preload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
**Serial lactate**: hypoperfusion, best predicts course and mortality; trend with capillary refill, urine output
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation
CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, IV access; **isotonic crystalloid** (balanced, 0.9% saline) before imaging; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + blood products** (emergency O-negative); crystalloid as bridge; no vasopressors
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone
Pulmonary edema after fluids → stop boluses, **inotrope**; children: epinephrine preferred, older exams may expect dopamine

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose
Isolated head injury: hypertension + bradycardia (Cushing); trauma hypotension + tachycardia → assume hemorrhage

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

sickle-cell-disease.name: Sickle cell disease
sickle-cell-disease.scope: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, stroke, sickle cell trait, hemoglobin electrophoresis
sickle-cell-disease.core: HbS polymerization causes chronic hemolysis and episodic vascular occlusion; fever, hypoxemia and focal neurologic deficits require urgent escalation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive β-globin disease; dehydration, hypoxemia, cold and infection trigger sickling
Functional asplenia → encapsulated infection from early childhood; **S. pneumoniae** leads pneumonia and fulminant sepsis

rows.label: Clues
items: Baseline anemia, reticulocytosis, jaundice; childhood dactylitis or recurrent severe bone pain
Acute chest syndrome: **new pulmonary infiltrate** plus fever, respiratory symptoms or hypoxemia
Sequestration: sudden splenomegaly, falling hemoglobin, shock; aplasia: **low reticulocyte count**, often parvovirus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes → rigid erythrocytes, endothelial injury, ischemia and shortened RBC survival
Acute chest trigger: **infection** most common; in situ thrombosis and fat embolism less often
Severe anemia → low viscosity, vasodilation, ↓afterload → **↑cardiac output** preserves oxygen delivery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC confirms genotype; newborn screen detects disease before symptoms
Crisis → CBC, reticulocytes, bilirubin; fever → blood cultures; respiratory symptoms → chest radiograph
New focal deficit → emergency brain imaging, without delaying transfusion preparation
Distinguish osteomyelitis from infarction using cultures and MRI when focal fever/pain persists

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain crisis → prompt **IV opioid**, morphine (AKI: lower dose or hydromorphone); no meperidine; NSAID only if kidneys normal
Pain crisis support: euvolemic hydration; oxygen only for hypoxemia; no routine transfusion
★ Acute chest → oxygen, **ceftriaxone + azithromycin**, incentive spirometry; transfuse for significant anemia
Severe acute chest, stroke → **urgent exchange transfusion**; sequestration (cautious) or aplasia → simple transfusion
Fever → immediate **IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime**, despite daily penicillin prophylaxis

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, avascular necrosis, priapism, pigment gallstones, nephropathy, retinopathy
Repeated transfusions → alloimmunization and iron overload; delayed hyperhemolysis can worsen anemia
Chronic hemolysis → ↑folate demand → **folate deficiency**, macrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Hydroxyurea** raises HbF, reduces crises; monitor CBC
Penicillin prophylaxis through age 5 in HbSS; pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib and influenza vaccines
Annual transcranial Doppler ages 2–16 in HbSS/HbSβ0; abnormal → chronic transfusion program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: persistent localized pain, fever; Salmonella or S. aureus
Iron deficiency: low ferritin, no hemolytic pattern

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.name: Skin and soft tissue infections
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.scope: Cellulitis, erysipelas, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, lymphangitis, necrotizing fasciitis
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.core: Skin infection management depends on purulence, systemic illness, and signs of deep tissue destruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin breaks, tinea pedis, edema/lymphedema, diabetes, obesity, injection drug use
Prior MRSA, crowding, recent hospitalization; surgery or penetrating trauma raises deep-infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Warmth, tenderness, erythema; rapidly expanding margins or systemic toxicity require urgent reassessment
★ **Pain out of proportion**, bullae, anesthesia, crepitus, shock → necrotizing infection
Perineal infection, especially diabetes → Fournier gangrene/necrotizing fasciitis; saltwater exposure → Vibrio, freshwater → Aeromonas

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonpurulent infection usually streptococcal, S aureus possible; purulent lesions usually S aureus
Fascial spread, toxins → necrosis, sepsis; minor trauma, no crepitus → **GAS**; crepitus → Clostridium/polymicrobial
Tinea pedis = portal of entry: acute fever/cellulitis is bacterial (S aureus/streptococcal) superinfection, not Trichophyton

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis; **bedside ultrasound** if occult fluid collection suspected
Culture drained pus for severe, recurrent, or resistant infection; blood cultures for systemic toxicity
Suspected necrotizing disease → immediate surgical evaluation; imaging must not delay exploration
Low laboratory risk score or absent gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Deep infection → **urgent debridement + vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam**, add clindamycin for toxin suppression
Confirmed group A streptococcal necrotizing infection → penicillin + clindamycin
Moderate cellulitis (systemic signs) → IV cefazolin; MRSA risk or cephalexin failure → vancomycin; severe → + pip-tazo
★ Abscess: add **antibiotics** for systemic signs, immunocompromise, extensive disease, or failed drainage
Pregnancy + suspected MRSA → clindamycin or vancomycin; **no doxycycline or fluoroquinolones**

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis; tissue loss and amputation
Toxic shock, multiorgan failure; recurrent cellulitis worsens lymphatic dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat interdigital fungal infection, manage edema, skin hygiene, protect wounds
Recurrent staphylococcal infections → consider nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine decolonization; avoid shared razors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stasis dermatitis: chronic, often bilateral, itchy
DVT: deep swelling without superficial spreading infection; contact dermatitis: pruritic exposure-pattern rash
Superficial thrombophlebitis: palpable indurated venous cord, not lymphatic streaks

table.title: Superficial patterns
rows: Incision and drainage; TMP-SMX if needed
Tender red streaks from skin break toward nodes
Usually S pyogenes; cephalexin; IV if systemic
Itchy follicular pustules on trunk/thighs after hot tub

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established IDSA-based infection management.

smoking-cessation.name: Smoking cessation
smoking-cessation.scope: Mortality reduction, 5 As counseling, pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement, bupropion, varenicline), behavioral programs
smoking-cessation.core: Stopping tobacco lowers cardiovascular, cancer (lung, oral cavity, bladder), pulmonary, and all-cause mortality at any age; counseling plus drugs produces the best quit rates.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **Ask every adult** about tobacco, vaping, dependence, prior attempts; include pregnancy
No readiness to quit → motivational interviewing; connect personal goals to cessation benefits
★ Smoking = **strongest modifiable** coronary, mortality risk; cessation beats statin, BP, glucose drugs

rows.label: Start/stop
items: 5 As: **Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange**; agree quit date, identify triggers
Arrange early follow-up, behavioral program, quitline; relapse → reassess triggers and renew treatment

rows.label: Test
items: Cigarettes/day, time to first cigarette, withdrawal; no routine biochemical confirmation
Check pregnancy, renal function, seizure/eating-disorder history before selecting drugs

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Nonpregnant adults → **varenicline or combination nicotine replacement** plus behavioral support
Pregnancy → counseling first; if unsuccessful, discuss drugs individually, evidence uncertain
COPD: **cessation alone slows FEV1 decline**, not inhaled steroids; oxygen helps only resting hypoxemia

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Psychiatric history alone does not contraindicate varenicline; monitor mood changes
E-cigarettes: insufficient USPSTF evidence for cessation; avoid recommending during pregnancy
Stopping smoke exposure reverses CYP1A2 induction → ↑clozapine/theophylline; nicotine not responsible

table.title: Drug selection
rows: Nausea, vivid dreams; renal dose adjustment
Irritation; safe in stable CAD; caution unstable ACS
Avoid seizures, eating disorders, abrupt alcohol withdrawal

soft-tissue-sarcoma.name: Soft tissue sarcoma
soft-tissue-sarcoma.scope: Liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, MRI of extremity, core needle biopsy, staging CT chest, surgical resection
soft-tissue-sarcoma.core: An enlarging deep soft-tissue mass, especially >5 cm, warrants imaging and planned biopsy through a sarcoma team.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior radiation, chronic lymphedema; NF1 and Li-Fraumeni increase susceptibility
Most cases sporadic; absence of pain or constitutional symptoms does not reassure

rows.label: Clues
items: Firm, progressive swelling; fixation, recurrence after excision, or rapid growth increases concern
Extremity lesions may compress nerves/vessels; retroperitoneal lesions present late with fullness or abdominal/back pain
Unexplained hematoma without trauma or one failing to resolve → reconsider tumor

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malignant mesenchymal proliferation; heterogeneous histologies require tissue classification
Spread predominantly hematogenous, especially to lungs; regional node involvement less typical than in carcinoma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI of extremity mass before biopsy** defines compartment, neurovascular relationships, and resection planning
Retroperitoneal mass → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis; superficial uncertain lump may start with ultrasound
★ **Image-guided core needle biopsy**; tract placed so it can be removed with definitive surgery
Avoid casual excision or transverse biopsy contaminating future surgical planes
★ **CT chest** for pulmonary staging, especially high-grade tumors; grade, size, site, metastases determine stage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized resectable disease → **wide surgical excision with negative margins**, usually limb-sparing
Radiotherapy before/after surgery for selected large, deep, high-grade, or margin-risk lesions
Amputation only when limb preservation cannot provide tumor control and useful function
Unresectable/metastatic disease → histology-directed systemic treatment; doxorubicin-based regimens often used
Selected isolated pulmonary metastases may be resected; multidisciplinary selection essential

rows.label: Complications
items: Local recurrence, lung metastases, loss of limb function; prognosis worsens with high grade and size
Radiation → fibrosis/edema; surgery → wound complications; doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: No population screening; unexplained enlarging lumps need early assessment
After treatment: clinical/local imaging and chest surveillance according to recurrence risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lipoma: soft, mobile, stable, homogeneous fat signal; atypical growth still needs evaluation
Abscess: inflammatory symptoms and fluid collection; atypical persistent lesions warrant tissue diagnosis
Hematoma: trauma/anticoagulation history and expected resolution over time

table.title: Common adult histologies
rows: Pleomorphic; often deep extremity in older adults

solid-organ-transplantation.name: Solid organ transplantation
solid-organ-transplantation.scope: Hyperacute rejection, acute allograft rejection, chronic allograft rejection, immunosuppressive regimens
solid-organ-transplantation.core: Allograft dysfunction requires urgent distinction among rejection, infection, obstruction/vascular failure, and immunosuppressant toxicity; biopsy usually establishes the rejection mechanism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HLA mismatch; sensitization after transplant, transfusion or pregnancy → preformed donor-specific antibodies
Missed immunosuppression, underdosing, drug interactions; rejection can occur late after medication withdrawal

rows.label: Clues
items: Kidney: ↑creatinine; liver: ↑bilirubin/enzymes; heart: ventricular dysfunction; lung: ↓spirometry
Fever, graft tenderness or malaise possible; rejection may be asymptomatic before laboratory abnormalities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allorecognition targets donor tissue; immunosuppression balances graft protection against infection and malignancy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Graft ultrasound/Doppler** when relevant → exclude obstruction, thrombosis or vascular compromise
Medication adherence/troughs, cultures and organ-specific viral testing; donor-specific antibodies assess humoral injury
★ **Allograft biopsy** distinguishes rejection from drug toxicity/infection; C4d may support antibody-mediated injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Common kidney maintenance: **tacrolimus + mycophenolate ± prednisone**; regimen varies by organ and risk
Induction in selected recipients → basiliximab or antithymocyte globulin
Steroid-resistant cellular rejection → antithymocyte globulin; coordinate all treatment with transplant team
Never reflexively escalate immunosuppression for unexplained fever before evaluating infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Calcineurin inhibitors → nephrotoxicity, hypertension, neurotoxicity; tacrolimus → diabetes
Mycophenolate → cytopenias, diarrhea, teratogenicity; sirolimus → poor wound healing, hyperlipidemia
Glucocorticoids → diabetes/osteoporosis; immunosuppression → opportunistic infection, skin cancer, EBV-related PTLD

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **ABO compatibility, HLA assessment, crossmatch** before transplant; lifelong adherence and trough monitoring
TMP-SMX prophylaxis for Pneumocystis; valganciclovir or preemptive monitoring for CMV according to risk
Vaccinate before transplant; avoid live vaccines during immunosuppression; sun protection and skin checks

rows.label: Mimics
items: Calcineurin toxicity: excessive exposure, no graft tenderness/enlargement; compatible biopsy, no alloimmune infiltrates
BK nephropathy: kidney transplant, viral PCR and viral inclusions on biopsy
Mechanical graft failure: obstruction/thrombosis demonstrated by imaging

table.title: Rejection patterns
rows: T-cell infiltrates; liver: portal eosinophils, endotheliitis

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics
Functional blindness: intact **pupillary reflex, threat blink, optokinetic nystagmus**
Extreme fever + normal pulse/labs → suspect falsification; **supervised rectal temperature** before antibiotics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic: **incompatible signs**: Hoover, give-way weakness, midline sensory split, forehead vibration discrepancy
Nonepileptic seizures: captured spell without **video-EEG** epileptiform change; often acute stressor
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression
Functional deficits → empathic explanation, expected recovery; nonepileptic seizures → **CBT**, no antiseizure drugs
